title: Fleming Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fleming wells have a 240 ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,400-$25,200.
h1: Fleming, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Fleming means looking closely at the well records before you rely on a listing’s water claim. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 240 feet, with the middle half between 188 and 280 feet. Reported yields are generally useful, with a 12.0 gpm median among the records that include pump-yield data.

The records are not complete for every well: 206 permits are on file, 125 are recorded as constructed, 139 report total depth, and only 45 report pump yield. Treat these figures as a strong local starting point, not a guarantee for a particular parcel.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Fleming?
sections.html:
Fleming-area wells commonly fall in the 100-to-300-foot range. That group accounts for 77% of the depth records. The median is 240 feet, and the middle half runs from 188 to 280 feet. For a drilling bid, that points to a fairly ordinary plains well rather than an automatic deep-hole project.

There is still meaningful variation. The 90th percentile is 322 feet, and the deepest record reaches 720 feet. Only 3% are under 100 feet, while 18% are between 300 and 600 feet and 2% exceed 600 feet. Local geology includes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, along with permits naming unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers and the Ogallala.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Fleming well make?
sections.html:
The reported yield numbers are favorable but come from only 45 wells. The median pump yield is 12.0 gpm, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. Among reported yields, 47% are in the 5-to-15 gpm range and another 47% are above 15 gpm.

No reported well is under 1 gpm, while 7% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. That does not make a high-producing well certain on a new lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the formation, and a buyer should ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any history of low pressure or seasonal shortage.

sections.heading: Fleming water levels: useful baseline, limited trend
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth from the ground surface down to the water when the well is not being pumped. The 13 Fleming-area records that report this measurement show a median of 152 feet, with the middle half between 116 and 187 feet. That baseline helps a driller plan casing, pump setting, and testing, but it is not the same as a guaranteed water level for an undeveloped parcel.

The permit file does not provide enough reported static-water measurements by decade to establish a reliable local rise or decline. Ask for recent measurements on the specific property and nearby wells. A pump test, well log, and comparison with wells near Haxtun or Crook can tell you more than the area median alone.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Fleming, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity in the area stretches back several decades, with the highest count in the 1990s at 42 permits. The record also includes 31 permits from the 2000s, 17 from the 2010s, and 11 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Older records can be incomplete, so the permit holder, driller, and construction status should be checked separately.

The most active drillers named in these records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc, with 27 records; Stewart Drilling Co., with 18; and Jim Feighny & Sons, with 8. Use these names as a research lead, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope, casing, grout, testing, and pump work before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new Fleming well cost?
sections.html:
For Fleming’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $8,400-$13,200. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $14,400-$25,200 at the median depth. A site with a deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, longer trenching, special casing or grout, or additional electrical work can move outside that range. Get a written bid that separates drilling from pump equipment, testing, trenching, power, permits, and any required treatment.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Fleming’s reported yields reduce one concern, but the dataset is not a promise for every lot. Only 45 wells report pump yield, and 67 of the 206 permits do not report total depth. Confirm that the well you are evaluating is actually constructed, properly permitted, and producing. A dry hole or weak-producing interval is a site-specific risk, especially where nearby records differ substantially.

Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles show 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 0 historic mine features, and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That is useful screening information, not a substitute for a water test. Test for bacteria, nitrate, and other contaminants appropriate to the property. Check septic setbacks, well access for a rig, power routing, casing and grout, and whether the proposed household use is allowed under the DWR permit.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Fleming lot
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the Colorado DWR permit and construction record for the property. Compare the well’s depth, aquifer, pump yield, static water level, use, and construction status with nearby records. The permit use mix includes domestic or household use on 60% of records and stock use on 58%; those categories can overlap, so do not assume a permit covers every use you want.

For a new build, have a driller review the lot before you finalize the house location, driveway, septic area, and utility route. An exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Budget from the completed-system range, then keep room for site-specific drilling, septic, electrical, and access work.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fleming, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Fleming is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 188 to 280 feet, and 77% of records are between 100 and 300 feet. Depth still varies: the deepest recorded well is 720 feet, so nearby well logs matter when estimating a new hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Fleming, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35-$55 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $8,400-$13,200. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,400-$25,200. A written bid should separate each part of the work.

faq.q: How much water do Fleming wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 45 Fleming-area records that report pump yield, the median is 12.0 gpm, with a middle half of 8.0-15.0 gpm. 47% report 5-15 gpm, and 47% report more than 15 gpm. These figures describe existing records, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Fleming, Colorado?
faq.a: Area mapping shows 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 0 historic mine features, and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That does not certify an individual well. Test the property’s water for bacteria, nitrate, and other locally appropriate contaminants before drinking it.

faq.q: Are Fleming well water levels going down?
faq.a: The 13 records with static water levels show a median depth to water of 152 feet, with a middle half from 116 to 187 feet. The available facts do not provide enough measurements by decade to establish a dependable falling trend. Request recent measurements and compare the specific well with nearby logs before buying.
